question_text: Solve dy/dx + y tan x = cos³x.

mark_split.label: Set up and simplify the integral

insider_note: cos³x/cos x simplifies to cos²x before integrating — students who try to integrate cos³x/cos x directly without cancelling the cos x first waste time on a much harder integral.

steps.label: Identify P and find ∫P dx
steps.margin_note: One mark. The equation is already in the standard linear form dy/dx + Py = Q.
steps.memory_tip: dy/dx + y tan x = cos³x is already the linear form — P is just the coefficient of y.
lines: Given D.E is dy/dx + y tan x = cos³x
This is in the form dy/dx + yP(x) = Q(x),
which is a linear D.E in y.
steps.why: Matching the equation against the standard linear form dy/dx + Py = Q identifies P and Q directly, and P must be integrated first because it feeds into the integrating factor.
common_mistakes: Taking P as cos³x (that is Q) instead of tan x.
Integrating tan x as −log(cos x) and forgetting it equals +log(sec x).

steps.label: Find the integrating factor
steps.margin_note: One mark. I.F. = e^(∫P dx) always — the formula never changes.
steps.memory_tip: e^(log(sec x)) = sec x — exponentiating a log of something returns that something.
lines: ∴ I.F. = e^(∫P dx) = e^(log(sec x)) = sec x
steps.why: The integrating factor for a linear equation is always e raised to the integral of P found in the previous step, and since e^(log A) = A, this simplifies directly to sec x.
common_mistakes: Writing the integrating factor as e^P instead of e^(∫P dx).
Leaving the answer as e^(log(sec x)) without simplifying it to sec x.

steps.label: Set up and simplify the integral
steps.margin_note: One mark. y·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)·Q dx is the standard linear-equation formula.
steps.memory_tip: cos³x/cos x cancels one power of cos x, leaving cos²x — always simplify before integrating.
lines: Hence, the solution is y·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dx
steps.why: The formula y·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dx applies directly once the integrating factor is known, and writing sec x as 1/cos x lets cos³x/cos x cancel to the much simpler cos²x before integrating.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to cancel cos x from the numerator and denominator, leaving a harder integral.
Multiplying sec x by cos³x incorrectly and losing a power of cos x.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Use cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2 to integrate, then multiply through by 2cos x to clear sec x.
steps.memory_tip: The double-angle identity cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2 is the standard way to integrate a plain cos²x.
lines: ⇒ y sec x = x/2 + sin2x/4 + c,
and multiplying through by 2 cos x:

lines.text: 2y = x cos x + sin x cos²x + c cos x

steps.why: The double-angle identity turns cos²x into a directly integrable sum, and multiplying the whole equation by 2cos x clears the sec x on the left and writes sin2x·cos x as sin x cos²x, giving the final boxed form the book marks.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the double-angle identity and trying to integrate cos²x directly, which is not a standard elementary antiderivative on its own.
Multiplying only the left side by 2cos x and forgetting to multiply every term on the right by the same factor.
